newsitem.title: INDIA: Price falls may fuel India's gold hunger.
newsitem.headline: Price falls may fuel India's gold hunger.

text.p: A downward trend in global gold prices could fuel India's hunger for the precious metal yet further in 1997, reinforcing the country's standing as the world's largest consumer, dealers and analysts said.
"I expect world gold prices to move in the range of US$355-$385 an ounce through next year compared to $360-$400 in 1996," said Makhan Lal Damani, president of the Bombay Bullion Association.
"More imports are expected if prices continue to rule low," Damani told Reuters.

Analysts say India's affinity to gold has turned it into the world's largest consumer of the metal, although nearly a third of its 900 million people live below the poverty line and the average per capita income is around $330 a year.
India's annual consumption of gold is estimated at around 500 tonnes, most of it imported. Official figures put the cost of gold imports in 1995 at $3.4 billion -- second only to oil.

India lifted a ban on gold imports in 1990 and gradually liberalised gold trade, allowing expatriate Indians to bring up to five kgs into the country once every six months, subject to a duty of 220 rupees ($6.1) per 10 grammes.
India's main demand for gold is in jewellery for the estimated 10 million weddings a year, which absorb nearly 300 tonnes of the metal, bullion dealers said.
India's wedding season, beginning in November and lasting up to February, is currently in full swing.

"There are so many weddings in a single day that I had to rush from one to another at breakneck speed," said jeweller Ajit Jain. He said gold imports would rise because of India's population growth and the role the metal played in people's lives.
"Wedding ceremonies and religious functions are there in larger numbers than before. The volumes are big, though quantities bought for each occasion are dwindling," Jain said.
Gold is regarded as security by rural dwellers, 70 percent of the population. It is also used as a hedge against inflation.
"Investment buying in gold has been declining," Jain said. "India's consumer goods' revolution, spread through television advertising, has left people with less money to buy gold."

India's gold holdings are put at around 9,000 tonnes, accumulated over centuries of trading, and account for about seven percent of an estimated world stock of 128,000 tonnes. These holdings mainly comprise family heirlooms and jewels given as part of dowries at weddings.
Top officials of the World Gold Council (WGC), who attended a seminar on gold in New Delhi in November, said India could use its dormant gold resources to develop a jewellery export sector.
"There is no reason, given India's infrastructure and its skills, why it should not be a major player in the gold export markets," WGC chief executive Elliot Hood told Reuters.
WGC economist George Milling-Stanley said developing countries, including India, were accounting for higher demand every year compared to their developed counterparts.
"This is partly because of thousands of years of affinity with gold. There is a real understanding of the value of gold in this part of the world," he said.
Indian officials who addressed the seminar promised to further liberalise gold imports and reduce customs duty.
"We are expecting some reduction in customs duty on gold, which would result in higher imports," said Jain.
Analysts said they believed India had the potential to step up its per capita gold consumption to one gramme (0.04 ounces) from the present 0.5 grammes (0.02 ounces).
"This would amount to a total consumption of 1,000 tonnes a year in the near future," said one. "It's mind-boggling."
Economic reforms, begun in 1991, have given growing buying power to India's estimated 200-million strong middle class.
"A part of the middle-class income will always come into gold," the analyst added.
